item.title: Debate: Should AI Write Our Emails?
item.summary: Two commentators argue about using AI assistants to write emails: efficiency against authenticity, and what happens to trust when any message might be generated.
item.transcript_text:
Sophie: Let me put my cards on the table. I use an AI assistant for most of my work emails now, and I don't feel the slightest bit guilty about it.
Rustam: I'm not asking you to feel guilty. I'm asking what we lose when nobody actually writes to anybody any more.
Sophie: Oh, come on, most emails aren't heartfelt letters. They're 'please find attached' and 'just following up'. If a machine can draft those in seconds, I've got more time for the work that matters.
Rustam: For routine messages, fine, I'll grant you that. But the line isn't nearly as clear as you're making it sound. A colleague who's just lost their job, a client who's upset, a thank-you to someone who went out of their way: those are emails too.
Sophie: And I'd write those myself. Nobody's suggesting we outsource sympathy.
Rustam: Aren't they, though? Once the tool is open and the draft is sitting there, looking perfectly reasonable, the temptation is just to hit send. Habits creep.
Sophie: That's a fair worry, but it's an argument for using the tool thoughtfully, not for refusing it altogether.
Rustam: My other concern is that people will start to discount everything they receive. If any message might have been generated, a kind word means less, because you can't be sure anyone actually meant it.
Sophie: Hmm, that's more persuasive, I'll admit. I've had messages from friends recently that were so smooth I found myself wondering whether they'd written a single word of them. And honestly, it took some of the warmth out. Maybe the answer is simply honesty, being open about when we've used it.
Rustam: Now that I could live with.
